snip.t: | Spirometry with bronchodilator | Is the defect obstructive, restrictive, or mixed? | Restrictive (↓FVC, normal/↑FEV₁/FVC) → pneumoconiosis; reversible obstruction → occupational asthma |
| Bronchial asthma exacerbation | Wheeze, reversible obstruction on spirometry, history of atopy; normal CXR | Predominant wheeze, rapid improvement with bronchodilators, absence of infiltrates |
Symptoms: episodic wheeze, cough (often at night or early morning), breathlessness, chest tightness; symptoms vary with time, triggers and season; improve with bronchodilators.
Spirometry: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with reversibility: FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 mL or more after a bronchodilator.

Bronchial smooth muscle – innervated by autonomic (parasympathetic → constriction) and sensory nerves (cough reflex).: Viral or irritant‑mediated inflammation releases acetylcholine and neuropeptides → bronchoconstriction and cough; bronchodilators act here.
Spirometry (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 = COPD); chest X-ray (increased bronchovascular markings, to exclude other causes); sputum culture in exacerbations; FBC (polycythaemia), ABG.
Spirometry (diagnostic): post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with symptoms and exposure.
Group A (few symptoms): a bronchodilator (short- or long-acting).

qs.q: A 30-year-old female presents for evaluation of chronic dry cough and breathlessness that worsen at night. Spirometry is performed before and after bronchodilator inhalation. Which spirometric finding confirms reversible airflow limitation diagnostic of asthma?
o: FEV1/FVC ratio remains strictly above 0.85 after bronchodilator use
FEV1 increases by more than 12% and more than 200 mL after salbutamol
FVC decreases significantly while FEV1 remains completely unchanged
FEV1 increases by exactly 5% and 100 mL following administration
qs.e: Reversibility is defined as an improvement in FEV1 by >12% and >200 mL after salbutamol administration. A ratio above 0.85 reflects normal spirometry rather than obstruction.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: During a respiratory ward round, a medical student asks about the exact spirometric criteria required to demonstrate significant bronchodilator reversibility in a patient with suspected asthma. What are the numerical thresholds?
o: FEV1 increase of greater than 12% and greater than 200 mL
FVC increase of greater than 20% and greater than 500 mL
FEV1 increase of greater than 5% and greater than 100 mL
PEF increase of greater than 10% and greater than 150 mL
qs.e: Significant reversibility in asthma is defined by an increase in FEV1 of more than 12% and an absolute increase of more than 200 mL following bronchodilator use. Lesser increases do not meet diagnostic thresholds for reversibility.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-year-old child with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis undergoes chest auscultation, revealing asymmetric low-pitched wheezes with a poor response to bronchodilators, alongside unequal breath sounds. Which complication best explains these findings?
o: Vertebral osteomyelitis
Pericardial effusion
Hilar lymphadenopathy
Tuberculous meningitis
qs.e: Enlarged hilar lymph nodes can compress bronchi, producing localized wheezing and altered breath sounds. The other conditions do not cause localized bronchial compression and asymmetric wheezing.

qs.q: According to current guidelines, what is the recommendation regarding the routine use of bronchodilator therapy in bronchiolitis?
o: It should be combined with ipratropium bromide for all patients
It is not supported as routine practice due to a lack of convincing evidence
It should be used routinely in all hospitalized infants
It is the primary intervention to improve oxygen saturation
qs.e: Bronchodilator therapy is not supported as routine practice by convincing evidence and was de-emphasized in updated guidelines due to lack of benefit exceeding potential harm. Selected patients may continue it only if they demonstrate clear clinical improvement.

qs.q: In the management of stable moderate to severe COPD, which class of long-acting bronchodilators includes agents such as tiotropium bromide?
o: Selective phosphodiesterase inhibitors reducing inflammation
Oral methylxanthine pro-drugs acting as bronchodilators
Long-acting anticholinergics including tiotropium bromide
Short-acting beta-2-agonists administered via inhaler devices
qs.e: Tiotropium bromide is a long-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator used in moderate to severe disease. Other long-acting options include beta-2-agonists such as salmeterol and formoterol.

qs.q: Which short-acting anticholinergic agent is commonly utilised as a bronchodilator in the management of milder cases of COPD?
o: Salbutamol sulphate
Tiotropium bromide
Salmeterol xinafoate
Ipratropium bromide
qs.e: Ipratropium bromide is a short-acting anticholinergic used in milder cases, alongside short-acting beta2-agonists like salbutamol. Tiotropium is a longer-acting anticholinergic.

qs.q: A patient with moderate to severe COPD experiences significant improvements in breathlessness despite minimal changes in post-bronchodilator FEV1 after starting a long-acting bronchodilator. How is this phenomenon viewed?
o: It represents a recognized and significant clinical benefit of therapy
It points to measurement error during spirometry testing
It suggests the patient has undiagnosed bronchial asthma instead
It indicates treatment failure requiring immediate withdrawal of the drug
qs.e: Significant improvements in breathlessness may be reported despite minimal changes in FEV1 during long-acting bronchodilator therapy. Breathlessness relief is a primary aim of COPD management.

qs.q: A 64-year-old woman with a history of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted to the hospital with an acute worsening of dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and purulent sputum. Aside from bronchodilators and antibiotics, which formulation of anti-inflammatory therapy is specifically indicated at this stage?
o: Intranasal steroid preparations
Intravenous cromolyn sodium
Oral or systemic corticosteroids
Inhaled high-dose fluticasone
qs.e: Oral or systemic corticosteroids are indicated to shorten recovery time during acute exacerbations. Inhaled corticosteroids are reserved for maintenance therapy rather than acute exacerbation management.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bronchodilators are drugs that relax airway smooth muscle to relieve bronchospasm. In East Africa they are used for asthma, COPD, and post‑viral wheeze, often with limited diagnostics. Clinicians must recognise reversible obstruction, choose the right agent, and monitor for side‑effects.

sections.p: Bronchodilators are medications that cause relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle, improving airflow. Diagnosis of an obstructive pattern is made by spirometry, but in many low‑resource settings a clinical diagnosis of wheeze with reversible symptoms is accepted.

t.b: An increase of >20 % indicates reversible bronchospasm.

sections.p: Asthma severity is staged by symptoms, nighttime awakenings, PEF variability, and need for rescue inhaler. COPD is staged by GOLD criteria (FEV1 % predicted).
b: Mild intermittent – symptoms <2 days/week, PEF >80 % predicted
Moderate persistent – symptoms >2 days/week, PEF 60‑80 % predicted
Severe persistent – daily symptoms, PEF <60 % predicted

sections.p: In East Africa the common triggers of bronchospasm are viral infections, indoor biomass smoke, allergic rhinitis, and HIV‑associated pulmonary disease. Exacerbations are often precipitated by malaria or diarrhoeal illness causing dehydration.

t.b: Normal or minimal bronchovascular markings in asthma; infiltrates suggest infection.
Positive acid‑fast bacilli or Gram‑positive cocci indicate alternative diagnosis.

sections.p: Patients present with episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal), chest tightness, and dyspnoea. In low‑resource settings, wheeze may be mistaken for malaria or pneumonia.
b: No fever or productive cough in pure asthma

t.b: Wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase, normal chest expansion.

sections.p: Spirometry with bronchodilator is the gold standard, but when unavailable, peak flow and clinical response to a SABA are used.

t.b: Normal in asthma; infiltrates suggest infection.
Positive AFB or Gram stain changes diagnosis.

sections.p: Severe bronchospasm, hypoxaemia, or failure to respond to SABA warrants urgent referral. Complications include pneumothorax from barotrauma and chronic airflow limitation.

t.b: <90 % requires supplemental oxygen and possible intubation.

sections.p: Treat the trigger, give a SABA for acute relief, then consider a LABA or inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) for maintenance. Anticholinergics are useful in COPD or severe asthma.
b: LABA (salmeterol) – add to SABA for persistent symptoms
Ipratropium – for COPD or severe asthma

t.b: Cost and need for inhaler technique; use only when benefit outweighs cost.
In COPD exacerbations or when β2‑agonists are contraindicated.

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, peak flow, and inhaler technique is essential. Preventive measures include avoiding biomass smoke, treating allergic rhinitis, and ensuring HIV viral suppression.

t.b: Poor technique reduces drug delivery, leading to uncontrolled symptoms.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress (SpO2 <90 %), inability to speak full sentences, persistent wheeze after SABA, sudden chest pain or haemoptysis

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in an acute asthma attack?
faq.a: A short‑acting β2‑agonist such as salbutamol inhaled via a metered‑dose inhaler or nebuliser.

faq.q: When can I use a long‑acting β2‑agonist?
faq.a: Only for patients with persistent symptoms despite a SABA; it should be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid.

faq.q: Why is theophylline rarely used now?
faq.a: It has a narrow therapeutic window, many drug interactions, and requires serum level monitoring, which is often unavailable.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with wheeze and nocturnal cough. She has no fever or sputum. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Asthma; look for reversible obstruction on spirometry or response to a SABA.
A patient with COPD exacerbation does not improve after 3 puffs of salbutamol. What is the next step? — Add ipratropium or consider antibiotics if infection suspected.
Why should inhaled corticosteroids be avoided in a patient with a history of tuberculosis? — They can worsen latent TB; ensure TB is treated before starting.
A child in a rural clinic has wheeze after a viral infection. The only available test is a peak flow meter. What does a >20 % rise after a SABA indicate? — Reversible bronchospasm, supporting asthma.
What is the main reason for using a spacer with a metered‑dose inhaler in low‑resource settings? — Improves drug delivery and reduces oral side‑effects.
A patient with severe asthma is on a SABA but still has nighttime symptoms. Which drug should be added? — A low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid.
When is a bronchodilator challenge test contraindicated? — In patients with severe hypoxaemia or hemodynamic instability.
